title: How to turn your study notes into audio and practice answers out loud
summary: Use an audio recap to hear the shape of your workflow, then practice with a spoken prompt and a silent answer interval.
body_markdown:
Use an audio recap to hear the shape of your workflow, then practice with a spoken prompt and a silent answer interval. Listening while reading along exercises a different skill from explaining a whole procedure from memory.


## My final is an oral check where I have to explain the whole workflow from memory. Is there a tool that can ask questions out loud from my study guide and make me explain my answer before showing the notes?


Educato offers paid live voice practice for answering questions aloud from your study material. For a rehearsal you can repeat word for word, use your phone's recorder. Write the workflow as a sequence of decisions. Record yourself giving just the opening condition. Pause playback and speak through the next decision, its rationale and the condition that would send you down a different branch. Listen back with the rubric open. A hesitation at a transition tells you where to start your next rehearsal.


### Build a prompt you can play with the screen face down


Choose a passage in your guide that ends with something you could hand in, such as a revised paragraph with a citation. Read it once and underline the words that change what you do next. Put the assignment on the front of a cue card. Put the decisions and the evidence your instructor expects on the back. Keep the front short enough to understand by ear. A long list of instructions can accidentally supply the entire answer.


Use your phone's recorder to read the front aloud and stop the recording at the question mark. Save the model answer separately so you decide when to hear it. You can play the question, put the phone down and take as long as the explanation needs. To capture your attempt on the same phone, let the question finish, then start a new recording. Give the attempt a name you can distinguish from the key when you return to it.


### Worked oral check: review a draft before submitting it


Suppose your writing instructor asks you to review a paragraph about a change to the school library. Your checklist asks three questions. Does the opening sentence identify the change? Does the meeting report support what the writer says about it? Can a reader find the passage? On the exam you get the draft and the report, but you have to recall the checklist yourself. Your examiner wants to hear what you would hand back and why.


Record this prompt. “The writer says the library added Saturday hours because students asked for them. The draft cites page three. Page four of the meeting report says the library will open on Saturdays starting in May. That's all the report says about the decision. Talk me through your review.” When you record your attempt, say the sentence you would hand back. That gives you something specific to compare with the passage afterward.


A first attempt might sound like this. “The paragraph identifies the new hours. I'd fix the page number and submit it.” Try reading the corrected sentence as the person marking it. You can now find the Saturday announcement on page four. Where on that page could you point to a student request? A correct page number can make a sentence look finished while part of its claim still needs evidence.


Here's one answer you could defend aloud. “I'd check the two parts of the opening sentence against the report. Page four gives me the new hours and the start month. It gives me no reason for the change, so I'd write, ‘The library will open on Saturdays starting in May,’ and cite page four. Before handing it back, I'd read the revised sentence with the report open and check that every detail is there.”


### Listen back with a pencil


Draw a line for each checklist question and write down the phrase in your recording that answers it. If all you can put beside the evidence check is “I'd look it up,” replay that part. Say exactly what you looked for and what you found. Then try the full prompt again. Can a listener tell why you changed the wording as well as the page number without having to interrupt you?


If you stall after saying “I'd turn to page four,” put a rescue cue on a spare card. Try “Which words in the draft still need proof?” Glance at it only when you get stuck. On the next attempt, turn the card over. Practice the short stretch from finding the passage to deciding what to revise before you spend another session rehearsing the opening.


### NotebookLM


NotebookLM’s Audio Overviews can turn sources into material for listening. Its mobile app supports downloaded overviews for offline listening. During rehearsal, pause at the start of a new step and describe what should come next before you continue the audio.[Read the product details](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/16213268?hl=en) .


For the library exercise, make an Audio Overview from your assigned guide to hear how the steps of draft review fit together. On the way to class, listen for the point where the reviewer has to decide whether to keep a claim. When you have a quiet place to speak, return to the recorded case. Give your own revised sentence aloud before you play the answer. That sentence is what your examiner could ask you to defend.


Choose the recorder when the timing of the reveal matters. You control the end of the question and can keep a separate key that matches your instructor's exact rubric. The tradeoff is writing your own follow-ups. A partner can supply variation by changing the opening situation or interrupting with a question about a phrase you cut. Give the partner the guide so they can tell whether an unexpected answer still meets its requirements.


### How do you know when to retire a prompt?


Change the entry point. Ask “What evidence would let you keep the reason in the original sentence?” Suppose page two now records that the library approved Saturday hours in response to a student petition. Explain which part of your revision you would undo, and where you would point a reader for each detail. If you still cut the reason out of habit, keep the prompt. Retire it when you can explain how the evidence changes your edit and still finish the submission check.
